fetched_contents.text: Predicting and Mitigating Freshmen Student Attrition: A Local-Explainable Machine Learning Framework Abstract With the emergence of novel methods for improving machine learning (ML) transparency, traditional decision-support-focused information systems seem to need an upgrade in their approach toward providing more actionable insights for practitioners. Particularly, given the complex decision-making process of humans, using insights obtained from group-level interpretation of ML models for designing individual interventions may lead to mixed results. The present study proposes a hybrid ML framework by integrating established predictive and explainable ML approaches for decision support systems involving the prediction of human decisions and designing individualized interventions accordingly. The proposed framework is aimed at providing actionable insights for designing individualized interventions. It was showcased in the context of college students’ attrition problem using a large and feature-rich integrated data set of freshman college students containing information about their demographics, educational, financial, and socioeconomic factors. A comparison of feature importance scores at the group- vs. individual-level revealed that while group-level insights might be useful for adjusting long-term strategies, using them as a one-size-fits-all strategy to design and implement individual interventions is subject to suboptimal outcomes. Keywords: Analytics, Prediction, Deep learning, SHAP, Explainable AI, Student attrition Introduction Machine learning (ML) methods, for a long time, have been known as black-box approaches with decent predictive accuracy but low transparency. Several approaches proposed in the literature (Carvalho et al., 2019; Gilpin et al., 2018) to interpret ML models and determine variables’ importance essentially provide high-level guidelines for practitioners based on the entire (average) sample characteristics. Whereas such guidelines could be informative and generalizable in contexts not involving humans as the decision-makers and role players (e.g., spam detection or classifying medical images) when it comes to predicting human behaviors and decisions, empirical generalizability of high-level one-size-fits-all interpretations is questionable. Particularly if such recommendations are to be used for designing and implementing individual-level intervention programs to change individuals’ mentality and persuade them not to act as predicted (by the ML model), it could lead to mixed results due to differences in variables’ importance at the group- vs. individual-level. Relying on a similar rationale, it has been shown in the biomedicine and healthcare analytics area that individual-level interpretations of the relative effect of features can result in more effective medical decisions (Ashley, 2016; Hodson, 2016). This has led to the emergence of a new area in healthcare analytics called precision medicine which generally aims to improve patient outcomes through individualizing diagnosis and treatment decisions (Kasztura et al., 2019). Additionally, human decision-making is typically a holistic process. That is, people either consciously or unconsciously tend to assess a given situation from multiple various angles before finalizing their decision in that regard. Hence, to realistically mimic that process using ML algorithms, they have to be fed with comprehensive and multifaceted data. College students’ attrition is one such decision-making process on which a large number of studies have been conducted using various statistical (Bai & Pan, 2009; Britt et al., 2017; Eng & Stadler, 2015; Zhang & Rangwala, 2018) and machine learning (Berens et al., 2018; Delen, 2010; Thammasiri et al., 2014) techniques to understand the contributing factors that lead students to quit college and help schools to take appropriate interventions. However, the factors identified in those studies resulted from analyzing data at the group level (i.e., across the entire sample of students), whereas at the individual level, each student who decides to drop out might have his/her reasons depending on his/her situation. Additionally, the focus in the prior studies is mostly on the personal (e.g., demographics), educational (e.g., GPA), and/or financial (e.g., loans) factors, while several socio-economic factors such as unemployment rate or income have been discussed in the literature as other likely influential considerations in making that decision. These factors, however, have never been studied using real-world data. According to the US Department of Education, around half of the dropouts among undergraduate students of the same cohort occur in the transition from the Freshman college year to the Sophomore year. A more recent report from the National Center for Education Statistics maintains that while 32.9% of undergraduates nationwide do not complete their degree programs, around three fourth of them (i.e., 24.1%) drop out after their freshman year (Hanson, 2022). Hence a great deal of effort by the schools’ administrations must be devoted to ensuring the retention of freshman students. Relatedly, many of the student retention/attrition studies (including this study) have focused on first-year attrition/dropouts (i.e., the number of students not returning for the second year). To address these gaps, the present study proposes a comprehensive hybrid framework by integrating state-of-the-art predictive ML methods and novel explainable machine learning approaches to improve proactive individualized human intervention programs. fetched_contents.text: Predictive modelling of student dropout risk: Practical insights from a South Korean distance university Abstract Distance education supports lifelong learning and empowers individuals in rapidly changing societal conditions, yet it encounters high dropout rates due to a range of individual and societal obstacles. This study addresses the challenge of creating a practical prediction model by analyzing extensive real-world time-point data from a well-established online university in Seoul. Covering 144,540 instances from 2018 to 2022, the study integrates diverse datasets to compare the accuracy of models based on longitudinal, semester-wise, and gender-specific datasets. The demographic, academic, and online metrics identified significant dropout indicators, including age (particularly when binned), residential area, specific occupations, GPA, and LMS log metrics, using a stepwise backward elimination process. The study revealed that, despite societal changes, recent data from the last four semesters can be effectively used for stable prediction training. Gender-based analysis showed different factors influencing dropout risk for males and females. The Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM) algorithm excelled in prediction accuracy, with the ROC-AUC metric affirming its superiority. However, logistic regression also showed its competitive performance and offered in-depth interpretation. In South Korea's distinct educational setting, merging advanced algorithms like LGBM with the interpretive strength of logistic regression is key for effective student support strategies. Keywords: Distance education, Dropout risk, Predictive modelling, Feature selection, Dataset modelling, Predictive algorithms 1. Introduction Learning impacts every pivotal moment of our lives. In today's fast-paced and ever-evolving world, the significance of lifelong learning has become increasingly crucial [1,2]. To remain competitive and relevant in an era of rapid technological advancements, relentless changes of the global economy, and shifting job markets, individuals must continuously adapt and acquire new skills throughout their personal and professional lives. Lifelong learning not only enriches knowledge and hones skills but also fosters personal growth, adaptability, and resilience, preparing individuals to face the uncertainties and complexities of the modern world. Utilizing digital platforms, distance universities have emerged as key enablers of lifelong learning, providing individuals with unprecedented access to diverse educational resources and learning opportunities [3]. By offering increased flexibility in terms of time and place, and fostering collaboration and networking among learners, digital platforms and online universities play a transformative role in promoting lifelong learning. They empower individuals to take ownership of their learning journey and adapt to the ever-changing demands of contemporary society, thereby contributing significantly to personal and professional growth. However, numerous challenges impede lifelong learning, and students who cease their education may encounter a wide array of disadvantages. Obstacles hindering lifelong learning can range from motivation deficits and financial constraints to time management difficulties and limited access to high-quality educational resources. As a result, students who discontinue their education risk stalling their career growth and social mobility, as well as experiencing adverse psychological effects such as diminished self-esteem and a sense of purpose. From an institutional standpoint, universities face the repercussions of high dropout rates, which can lead to reduced retention rates, decreased funding, and reputational damage [4]. These factors may impact their ability to attract new students, retain existing ones, and maintain their academic standing. Despite their convenience and growing popularity, student dropout is a particularly serious problem in online universities. According to the South Korean government's Public Disclosure Information of Higher Education in Korea, as of 2022, there are 18 distance universities with a total enrolment of 277,874 students. However, the dropout rate in these universities is notably higher at 16.41 %, compared to the 5.97 % at offline universities (calculated from [5]). Consequently, enhancing student retention has become a critical concern for educational institutions, particularly in the realm of online learning. Learning analytics is getting attention as a key to addressing this problem among others. Recent advancements in learning analytics along with the proliferation of digital technologies offer new opportunities for educational institutions to monitor, analyse, and support students throughout their academic journey. By leveraging learning analytics, universities can glean insights into student behaviour, engagement, and performance. This allows them to customize their interventions, support strategies, and learning pathways, catering to the diverse needs of individual learners ([6]; Siemens, 2013 [7]). Given these challenges and opportunities, both forecasting and early support in online education have gained prominence. Developing predictive models to learn a student's risk of dropping out allows universities to proactively provide targeted support and resources, thereby enhancing retention rates and promoting student success [8,9,10]. Sequential decision-making in higher education attrition is best understood as a stage-specific process in which students move through enrollment, first-year, sophomore, senior, and postgraduate stages, with attrition risk and continuation likelihood changing across each phase. The theoretical framework evidence suggests a phase-orientated view of student retention and attrition, distinguishing successive stages in the decision to leave or change course, including initial non-... and later transition points [N1-R1]. The empirical evidence reinforces that attrition is not a single event but a series of decisions, with the first year especially salient in the literature on student attrition and retention [N1-R5]. In the empirical study on freshman attrition, the authors note that “around half of the dropouts among undergraduate students of the same cohort occur in the transition from the Freshman college year to the Sophomore year” and that 24.1% of undergraduates nationwide drop out after their freshman year [N2-F2]. This implies that first-year-to-sophomore transition is one of the most predictive attrition points in the undergraduate journey.

The evidence also identifies transition points that are especially relevant for predicting continuation or leave decisions. In the graduate student retention study, the authors used logistic regression to predict whether students successfully completed their degree, with the dichotomous dependent variable representing degree completion or attrition [N2-F1]. For master’s students, significant predictors included higher graduate GPA, increased time in the program, increased funding from all sources, and full- or part-time registration status in coursework-only or coursework-plus-major-research-paper programs [N2-F1]. For doctoral students, only increased time in the program and increased funding from all sources significantly increased the chances of graduation [N2-F1]. This suggests that attrition risk is especially strong when students face longer time-to-degree pressures and insufficient financial support, and that these factors matter differently at the master’s versus doctoral stage.

Stage-specific contextual factors are central to explaining why students continue or leave. The theoretical framework evidence points to workload, financial pressure, academic support, and social integration as important elements of the decision process [N1-R1]. The empirical evidence supports this by showing that financial support variables, such as funding received from internal and external scholarships and assistantships, were used as independent variables in graduate retention analysis [N2-F1]. It also emphasizes that attrition is influenced by the institutional environment and that universities must account for the costs of admission, planning, and lost income, as well as the impact of financial support on incoming students [N2-F1]. The freshman attrition study similarly highlights demographic, educational, financial, and socioeconomic factors as contributing to the decision to leave, with the authors noting that prior studies focused mostly on personal, educational, and financial factors, while socio-economic factors such as unemployment rate or income were also discussed as likely influential considerations [N2-F2]. This indicates that attrition is shaped by stage-specific pressures that vary across enrollment, first year, sophomore year, senior year, and postgraduate stages.

Overall, the stage-specific decision process in higher education attrition can be described as a sequence of transitions in which students face different combinations of workload, financial pressure, academic support, and social integration. The first year and the transition from freshman to sophomore are especially predictive of attrition, while later stages such as master’s and doctoral programs are associated with time-to-degree pressures and funding adequacy. Logistic regression and related empirical methods are used to operationalize these stage-specific predictors into models of continuation or leave, but the evidence also suggests that the decision process is not captured fully by a single-stage model alone [N2-F1][N2-F2].

Sequential logistic regression models for student attrition are structured differently from single-stage logistic regression because they explicitly account for the fact that student decisions are not fixed at one point in time but occur across multiple stages. The methodological evidence emphasizes that sequential decision-making involves stage-specific predictors and time-varying covariates, and that incorporating time-dependent covariates can improve predictive performance [N3-R1]. In the context of attrition prediction, this means that a model should not treat each student as a single observation with one outcome; instead, it should allow for changes in predictors and outcomes as students move through enrollment, first year, sophomore year, senior year, and postgraduate stages.

A single-stage logistic regression model is typically used when the outcome is observed once and the predictors are static or only partially time-varying. In contrast, sequential logistic regression can be specified as a series of models at each stage, or as a joint model that estimates parameters across stages using an optimization algorithm with regularizers [N3-R3]. The evidence also supports the use of longitudinal and time-to-event approaches when the focus is on attrition timing and censoring, indicating that sequential models should be paired with careful handling of time-dependent variables rather than treated as a simple extension of single-stage regression [N4-R5]. For attrition prediction, this matters because students may change course, withdraw, or complete their degree at different points in the educational journey, and the covariates that influence those decisions can vary across stages.

Handling time-varying and stage-specific covariates is a central methodological challenge. The evidence shows that time-varying covariates can be incorporated into machine learning and survival modeling approaches, and that using such covariates can improve predictive performance [N3-R1]. In educational attrition analysis, this means including variables that change as students progress through the program, such as GPA, funding status, enrollment status, and online metrics, as well as stage-specific factors such as first-generation status, organizational involvement, and demographic characteristics [N3-R2][N4-F3]. The South Korean distance university study provides a concrete example of how longitudinal, semester-wise, and gender-specific datasets can be used to identify dropout indicators, with age, residential area, occupation, GPA, and LMS log metrics emerging as significant predictors [N4-F3]. This implies that sequential logistic regression models should be built with time-varying covariates and stage-specific variables rather than relying on a single snapshot of student characteristics.

Interpretation of coefficients and predicted probabilities across stages is more complex than in a single-stage model. In logistic regression, coefficients represent the log odds of the outcome given a unit change in the predictor, but in sequential modeling, these effects may vary by stage and may depend on the timing of the measurement event [N3-R3]. The empirical evidence also shows that outcome coding and baseline modeling strategy matter: the graduate student retention study used a dichotomous dependent variable indicating whether the student successfully completed the degree, while the freshman attrition study compared feature importance scores at the group- vs. individual-level and emphasized that individual-level interpretations are important for designing interventions [N2-F1][N2-F2]. For sequential models, this means that predicted probabilities should be interpreted conditionally on the student’s current stage, and that stage-specific coefficients should be reported alongside stage-specific predicted probabilities to avoid misinterpretation. Overall, sequential logistic regression is better suited than single-stage models to explain and predict attrition across multiple stages when the decision process is genuinely sequential and when predictors change over time [N3-R1][N3-R3].

A good prediction model for student continuation/leave decisions should be built around a clear outcome coding and a baseline modeling strategy that matches the research question. The empirical evidence shows that logistic regression is often used as a dichotomous outcome model, with the dependent variable representing whether the student continues or leaves [N2-F1]. In the graduate student retention study, the dependent variable was whether the student successfully completed the degree, making it a classic binary outcome model [N2-F1]. The freshman attrition study similarly used a classification framework in which students were categorized based on demographic, educational, financial, and socioeconomic factors, with the outcome being attrition or retention [N2-F2]. This suggests that outcome coding should be straightforward and aligned with the administrative or academic definition of continuation versus leave.

Baseline modeling strategy should be chosen carefully based on the data and the research goals. The evidence supports using logistic regression as a baseline model when the goal is to interpret relationships and weights, since logistic regression produces outputs that show the relationship between predictors and the outcome along with weights to the outcome categories [N5-R2]. However, the empirical evidence also indicates that more complex models such as decision trees, neural networks, and hybrid explainable machine learning approaches are frequently compared against logistic regression for attrition prediction [N2-R3][N2-F2]. This implies that logistic regression should be used either as a baseline for comparison or as an interpretable anchor model when the priority is transparency rather than purely predictive performance.

Validation methods are essential for assessing whether the model will generalize to new data. The evidence explicitly mentions cross-validation and holdout testing as important validation approaches [N4-R5]. The freshman attrition study emphasizes that group-level insights may be useful for long-term strategies, but they should not be used as a one-size-fits-all strategy for individual interventions, and it stresses the importance of using both group- and individual-level interpretations [N2-F2]. The predictive modeling literature in higher education also emphasizes the need for practical prediction models that are validated against real-world data [N4-F3]. Together, these sources support a validation strategy that combines internal validation such as cross-validation with external holdout testing, and that explicitly accounts for the difference between group-level generalizability and individual-level applicability [N2-F2][N4-R5].

Model performance metrics should be selected to reflect the relevance of attrition prediction. The empirical evidence highlights accuracy, feature importance, and predictive performance as important metrics [N2-R2][N2-F2]. The South Korean distance university study reports ROC-AUC as a metric affirming the superiority of the Light Gradient Boosting Machine algorithm, while also noting that logistic regression remained competitive and offered in-depth interpretation [N4-F3]. This indicates that attrition prediction should not be judged solely by overall accuracy; instead, metrics such as ROC-AUC, precision, recall, and F1 should be considered, especially when the outcome is imbalanced. The literature also emphasizes that predictive models should be evaluated for their ability to support actionable interventions, not just for statistical fit [N2-F2]. Taken together, a good model should be built on a clear outcome coding and baseline strategy, validated using cross-validation and holdout testing, and assessed with metrics that are relevant to attrition prediction and institutional action [N5-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3].

Longitudinal and time-to-event methods differ from sequential logistic regression in educational attrition analysis primarily because they are designed to handle attrition timing, censoring, and the dynamic nature of student decisions. The evidence shows that survival analysis techniques are powerful for modeling educational event occurrences because they can capture the time-dependent nature of retention and completion [N6-R1]. The survival analysis of transfer students paper explicitly states that survival analysis offers a nuanced approach to examining the time-dependent nature of student retention and completion, allowing for the inclusion of both time-to-event and censoring information [N6-R2]. In contrast, sequential logistic regression is typically used when the focus is on stage-specific decisions at multiple points in time, but it may not fully capture the timing and censoring structure that is central to attrition modeling [N6-R1][N6-R2].

Time-to-event modeling is more appropriate for attrition when the research question is not only whether a student leaves but when they leave and how the timing depends on covariates. The survival analysis evidence explains that survival models estimate the time until an event of interest and model longitudinal data where the outcome is the time until an occurrence of an event [N6-R3]. The survival analysis framework for early prediction of student dropout further clarifies that survival models are used to estimate time to events of interest, and that the ability to model the dynamic nature of student dropout is a key advantage [N6-R4]. This makes time-to-event modeling especially suitable for attrition prediction because students may be censored if they do not leave before the end of the observation period, and the timing of the event is often crucial for understanding why students continue or leave [N6-R1][N6-R2].

Longitudinal models also handle repeated events and competing risks more naturally than sequential logistic regression. The evidence indicates that survival analysis can be used for repeated events and that longitudinal data structures are central to the method [N6-R1][N6-R3]. The Cox proportional hazards model is specifically cited as a survival analysis framework for early prediction of student dropout, which implies that it can accommodate multiple events and competing risks by estimating hazard functions rather than just binary outcomes [N6-R5]. In contrast, sequential logistic regression may require multiple separate models at each stage or an ad hoc way of handling repeated events, which can make the model less flexible and harder to interpret [N3-R3][N6-R1]. The evidence also suggests that longitudinal models can be extended to handle time-varying covariates, which is a key advantage in educational attrition analysis [N6-R2][N6-R3].

The trade-offs between interpretability, flexibility, and computational complexity are important. Logistic regression is highly interpretable because it provides coefficients that can be directly linked to the log odds of the outcome [N5-R2]. However, it is less flexible than time-to-event or longitudinal methods when the research question involves attrition timing, censoring, repeated events, or competing risks [N6-R1][N6-R3]. Time-to-event and longitudinal models, especially survival models such as Cox regression, are more flexible because they can incorporate time-dependent covariates and model the timing of the event [N6-R2][N6-R5]. The evidence also shows that machine learning and deep learning approaches can improve predictive performance when time-dependent covariates are incorporated, but they often sacrifice interpretability for flexibility and complexity [N3-R1][N4-F3]. In educational attrition analysis, this means that a good model should balance interpretability with the need to capture timing, censoring, and stage-specific dynamics [N5-R2][N6-R1][N6-R5].

This stage-specific structure is central to understanding why some students continue and others leave: the decision to persist or withdraw is shaped by changing workload, financial pressure, academic support, and social integration across the educational journey [N1-R1][N2-F1][N2-F2].

## 1) How the stage-specific decision process works across higher education
The evidence suggests that continuation and leave decisions are not uniform across stages. The theoretical framework points to successive stages in the decision to leave or change course, including initial non-... and later transition points [N1-R1]. Empirically, the literature emphasizes that attrition is especially concentrated in transition periods. In one study, about half of undergraduate dropouts occur in the transition from freshman to sophomore year, and 24.1% of undergraduates nationwide drop out after their freshman year [N2-F2]. For graduate students, attrition is also strongly influenced by time in the program and funding; master’s students showed significant improvements in degree completion with higher graduate GPA, longer time in the program, and increased funding from all sources, while doctoral students had only increased time in the program and increased funding as significant predictors [N2-F1]. This shows that attrition is not only a matter of whether a student leaves, but also of when and under what conditions.

Stage-specific contextual factors are crucial. The evidence repeatedly points to workload, financial pressure, academic support, and social integration as important determinants [N1-R1]. In graduate retention analysis, financial support variables such as scholarships, assistantships, and internal/external funding were used as predictors [N2-F1]. The freshman attrition study similarly notes that demographic, educational, financial, and socioeconomic factors are important, with prior studies often focusing on personal, educational, and financial variables while also acknowledging socio-economic factors such as unemployment rate or income [N2-F2]. This indicates that the decision process is shaped by the student’s environment at each stage rather than by a single snapshot of characteristics.

## 2) How sequential logistic regression models are structured
Sequential logistic regression differs from single-stage logistic regression because it explicitly accounts for the fact that student decisions occur across multiple stages. The methodological evidence says that sequential decision-making involves stage-specific predictors and time-varying covariates, and that incorporating time-dependent covariates can improve predictive performance [N3-R1][N3-R3]. In attrition prediction, this means the model should not treat each student as a single observation with one outcome; instead, it should allow for changes in predictors and outcomes as students move through enrollment, first year, sophomore year, senior year, and postgraduate stages.

A single-stage logistic regression model is typically used when the outcome is observed once and the predictors are static or only partially time-varying. In contrast, sequential logistic regression can be specified as a series of models at each stage, or as a joint model that estimates parameters across stages using an optimization algorithm with regularizers [N3-R3]. The evidence also suggests that longitudinal and time-to-event approaches are especially relevant when the focus is on attrition timing and censoring, indicating that sequential models should be paired with careful handling of time-dependent variables rather than treated as a simple extension of single-stage regression [N4-R5].

Handling time-varying and stage-specific covariates is a central methodological challenge. The evidence shows that time-varying covariates can be incorporated into machine learning and survival modeling approaches, and that using such covariates can improve predictive performance [N3-R1]. In educational attrition analysis, this means including variables that change as students progress through the program, such as GPA, funding status, enrollment status, and online metrics, as well as stage-specific factors such as first-generation status, organizational involvement, and demographic characteristics [N3-R2][N4-F3]. The South Korean distance university study provides a concrete example of how longitudinal, semester-wise, and gender-specific datasets can be used to identify dropout indicators, with age, residential area, occupation, GPA, and LMS log metrics emerging as significant predictors [N4-F3].

## 3) How sequential logistic regression is interpreted across stages
Interpretation of coefficients and predicted probabilities is more complex in sequential models than in a single-stage model. In logistic regression, coefficients represent the log odds of the outcome given a unit change in the predictor, but in sequential modeling, these effects may vary by stage and may depend on the timing of the measurement event [N3-R3]. The empirical evidence also shows that outcome coding and baseline modeling strategy matter: the graduate student retention study used a dichotomous dependent variable indicating whether the student successfully completed the degree, while the freshman attrition study compared feature importance scores at the group- vs. individual-level and emphasized that individual-level interpretations are important for designing interventions [N2-F1][N2-F2]. For sequential models, this means that predicted probabilities should be interpreted conditionally on the student’s current stage, and that stage-specific coefficients should be reported alongside stage-specific predicted probabilities to avoid misinterpretation.

## 4) What makes a good prediction model for continuation/leave decisions
A good prediction model should be built around a clear outcome coding and a baseline modeling strategy that matches the research question. The empirical evidence shows that logistic regression is often used as a dichotomous outcome model, with the dependent variable representing whether the student continues or leaves [N2-F1]. In the graduate student retention study, the dependent variable was whether the student successfully completed the degree, making it a classic binary outcome model [N2-F1]. The freshman attrition study similarly used a classification framework in which students were categorized based on demographic, educational, financial, and socioeconomic factors, with the outcome being attrition or retention [N2-F2]. This suggests that outcome coding should be straightforward and aligned with the administrative or academic definition of continuation versus leave.

Baseline modeling strategy should be chosen carefully based on the data and the research goals. The evidence supports using logistic regression as a baseline model when the goal is to interpret relationships and weights, since logistic regression produces outputs that show the relationship between predictors and the outcome along with weights to the outcome categories [N5-R2]. However, the empirical evidence also indicates that more complex models such as decision trees, neural networks, and hybrid explainable machine learning approaches are frequently compared against logistic regression for attrition prediction [N2-R3][N2-F2]. This implies that logistic regression should be used either as a baseline for comparison or as an interpretable anchor model when the priority is transparency rather than purely predictive performance.

Validation is essential for assessing whether the model will generalize to new data. The evidence explicitly mentions cross-validation and holdout testing as important validation approaches [N4-R5]. The freshman attrition study emphasizes that group-level insights may be useful for long-term strategies, but they should not be used as a one-size-fits-all strategy for individual interventions, and it stresses the importance of using both group- and individual-level interpretations [N2-F2]. The predictive modeling literature in higher education also emphasizes the need for practical prediction models that are validated against real-world data [N4-F3]. Together, these sources support a validation strategy that combines internal validation such as cross-validation with external holdout testing, and that explicitly accounts for the difference between group-level generalizability and individual-level applicability [N2-F2][N4-R5].

Model performance metrics should be selected to reflect the relevance of attrition prediction. The empirical evidence highlights accuracy, feature importance, and predictive performance as important metrics [N2-R2][N2-F2]. This indicates that attrition prediction should not be judged solely by overall accuracy; instead, metrics such as ROC-AUC, precision, recall, and F1 should be considered, especially when the outcome is imbalanced. The literature also emphasizes that predictive models should be evaluated for their ability to support actionable interventions, not just for statistical fit [N2-F2]. Taken together, a good model should be built on a clear outcome coding and baseline strategy, validated using cross-validation and holdout testing, and assessed with metrics that are relevant to attrition prediction and institutional action [N5-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3].
